Atom. They are the smallest units of matter that retain the identity of a chemical element, consisting of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by a cloud of electrons. The building blocks of all ordinary matter, atoms combine through chemical bonding to form molecules and extended structures. Modern atomic theory emerged from Rutherford's gold-foil experiment in nineteen oh-nine, which revealed that atoms are mostly empty space with a dense, positively charged nucleus.

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons and holds ninety-nine point nine percent of the atom's mass in a volume of roughly ten to the minus fifteen meters. Electrons orbit at approximately ten to the minus ten meters radius. Atomic number, abbreviated Z, equals the number of protons and determines element identity and chemical properties. Mass number, abbreviated A, equals protons plus neutrons and defines the isotope and determines atomic mass approximately. Electrons occupy orbitals arranged in shells—K, L, M, and so on—according to quantum mechanics, not the classical planetary model Bohr proposed.

Chemical properties arise from valence electrons in the outermost shell. Filled shells are stable and confer chemical inertness, as seen in noble gases. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different neutron counts. They vary in mass but have identical chemistry. Atoms are bound together by the electromagnetic force attracting the nucleus and electrons, while the strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together. Atoms are mostly empty space. The electron probability cloud defines the effective atomic radius, not a solid boundary.

Ionization removes one or more electrons, creating positively charged cations. Gaining electrons forms negatively charged anions. Atomic radius trends show an increase down a group as more electron shells appear, and a decrease across a period as increased nuclear charge pulls electrons closer. Electronegativity measures the tendency to attract electrons, and ionization energy measures the energy required to remove an electron. Both vary systematically across the periodic table and determine chemical reactivity and bonding type. The periodic table organization reflects electronic structure. Groups share valence-electron configuration, explaining recurring chemical properties like the inertness of noble gases and the reactivity of halogens. Modern atomic theory reconciles quantum mechanics with classical observation, showing that atoms are stable, discrete entities despite being mostly empty space.
